---
title: "Repository & Project Structure"
order: 1
---

### S1 — One repo per project, not per person

The work survives the author leaving. Code belongs to the project, not to whoever wrote it. When someone graduates, their scripts stay findable and runnable instead of disappearing onto a personal laptop.

```
adamolab/                  # one GitHub org
├── reaction-time-study/   # one repo per project
├── eye-tracking-2026/
└── saccade-model/
```

### S2 — Standard top-level layout

You find things without asking anyone. Give every repo the same skeleton: README, data/, src/, results/, and an environment lock. Open any project and you know where the code, data pointers, and outputs live.

```
saccade-model/
├── README.md
├── data/            # or a pointer to storage
├── src/
├── results/
└── environment.yml
```

### S3 — No data committed to git

Git chokes on large binaries. Git diffs text well and binaries badly. Commit a few gigabytes and clones crawl, history bloats, and you cannot rewind. Keep data in real storage and version it with a tool built for the job.

```bash
# .gitignore
data/
*.h5

# version data with DVC instead of git
dvc add data/raw.h5
```

### S4 — README answers three questions

New members onboard without you. Cover what the project is, how to set up the environment, and how to run it end to end. A newcomer should reach a first result without messaging you.

```markdown
# Saccade Model
**What:** fits saccade latency from eye-tracking data.
**Setup:** `conda env create -f environment.yml`
**Run:** `make all`
```
